The Antarctic lanternfish Electrona antarctica exhibits pronounced sexual size dimorphism, a trait that has been documented through extensive trawl surveys in the Southern Ocean. Adult females reach a maximum standard length of 11.5 centimeters [Li = 11.5 centimeters], a value derived from field measurements of gravid individuals captured during the austral summer. Males, by contrast, attain a significantly smaller ultimate standard length of 10.3 centimeters [Li = 10.3 centimeters], a difference of over one centimeter that likely reflects differential investment in gamete production between the sexes. The onset of sexual maturation in this species is associated with the attainment of a standard length of 7.4 centimeters [Lp = 7.4 centimeters] at puberty, a threshold that many individuals reach during their second or third year of life depending on local productivity regimes. These size parameters are consistent with the general myctophid pattern of moderate body size and pronounced female-biased growth, which has been confirmed by multiple otolith-based aging studies across the Scotia Sea and the Weddell Gyre.
